explanations.explanation: White occupies the center and controls d5. The pawn move also opens diagonals for the queen and king’s bishop.
Black matches White’s central presence and controls d4. The e5 pawn is undefended for now, so White can develop while attacking it.
White develops a knight, attacks the e5 pawn, and supports d4. Moving the knight also clears a square needed for kingside castling.
Black develops the knight to defend e5 and also controls d4. White can develop a bishop or challenge the center with d4.
White develops the bishop toward f7, a pawn defended only by the king. White is ready to castle and may later build a pawn center with c3 and d4.
White’s bishop pressures the knight that defends e5. Capturing the knight does not immediately win the pawn, but the pressure can support White’s central plans.
Black uses the c-pawn to control d4 without mirroring White’s central pawn. A later exchange on d4 can leave Black with an extra central pawn.
Black prepares ...d5 with pawn support, challenging White’s center. The trade-off is that the e6 pawn restricts Black’s light-squared bishop.
Black prepares ...d5 with support from the c-pawn. Unlike ...e6, this leaves a diagonal open for the c8 bishop, but the c6 pawn occupies the knight’s usual square.
Black immediately attacks the e4 pawn. After the common exd5, an early queen recapture can let White develop a piece while attacking the queen.
Black’s d-pawn controls e5, preparing ...Nf6. Black often follows with ...g6 and ...Bg7, aiming at the center from a distance.
Black develops a knight and immediately attacks e4. White can gain space with e5, but Black hopes to challenge an advanced pawn center later.
White occupies the center, controls e5, and opens a diagonal for the c1 bishop. The queen already supports the d4 pawn.
Black claims central space and controls e4, making it harder for White to establish pawns on both d4 and e4. White can challenge the d5 pawn with c4.
White offers the c4 pawn to draw Black’s d-pawn away from the center. Black can accept with ...dxc4 or support the d5 pawn instead.
Black develops a knight and controls e4 without committing a central pawn. Black keeps the option of challenging White’s center with pieces or pawns.
White gains queenside space and adds control of d5. The c-pawn has moved before the knight develops to c3, leaving both pieces flexible.
White controls d5 from the flank and keeps several central pawn formations available. The position can later transpose into a 1. d4 opening.
White develops a knight and controls e5 while postponing a central pawn move. This flexible start can lead to several different openings.
White develops the knight and supports d4. A common plan is d4, meeting ...cxd4 with Nxd4 to open the center.
Black supports the c5 pawn and controls e5. This prepares ...Nf6 while leaving several Sicilian systems available.
Black develops the knight and adds pressure on d4. Black keeps the option of playing ...d5 in one move rather than committing the d-pawn now.
Black opens a diagonal for the dark-squared bishop and prepares ...d5. White can still pursue the open Sicilian with d4.
White uses the c-pawn to support d4. If Black exchanges on d4, White may be able to recapture with the c-pawn and establish a broad center.
White builds a center with pawns on e4 and d4 and opens lines for development. Black has prepared ...d5 to challenge it.
Black uses the d5 pawn to attack the e4 pawn. White can advance it, exchange on d5, or develop a piece to support the center.
White gains space and controls f6, restricting Black’s kingside knight. Black commonly challenges the base of the pawn chain with ...c5.
White establishes a second central pawn. Black usually follows through with ...d5, supported by the c6 pawn.
Black attacks e4 with the c6 pawn supporting d5. White can advance, exchange, or develop a defender.
White advances the e-pawn to gain space. Black often develops the c8 bishop before playing ...e6, or immediately challenges the center with ...c5.
White captures in the center. Black can recover the pawn on d5 immediately with the queen or delay the recapture while developing a knight.
Black recovers the pawn with the queen. White can develop Nc3 with an attack on the queen, gaining time as it moves away.
White develops a knight while attacking the queen. Black must choose a safe square for the queen, commonly a5, d6, or d8.

explanation.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5
explanation.title: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano

explanations.explanation: Black develops the bishop to c5 and keeps the knight free to develop later. White can prepare a central d4 advance or choose a quieter setup with d3.

explanation.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6
explanation.title: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense

explanations.explanation: Black develops a knight and attacks e4. White can defend the pawn or counterattack, for example by directing a knight toward f7.

explanation.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6
explanation.title: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense

explanations.explanation: Black’s a-pawn attacks the bishop. White must decide whether to exchange on c6 or retreat and preserve the bishop.

explanation.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4
explanation.title: Ruy Lopez: 4. Ba4

explanations.explanation: White preserves the bishop and keeps pressure on the c6 knight, a defender of e5. Black can develop the kingside or later challenge the bishop with ...b5.

explanation.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6
explanation.title: Ruy Lopez: 4...Nf6

explanations.explanation: Black develops and attacks e4. White can defend the pawn or continue developing; castling is a common choice.
White immediately challenges e5 and aims to open the center. Black commonly exchanges on d4.
Instead of defending e5, Black develops and counterattacks e4. Both central pawns are under attack, and White can capture on e5 or defend their own pawn.
Black defends e5 with a pawn. The structure is solid, though the d6 pawn limits the f8 bishop and Black has yet to develop a piece.
White develops a knight and supports e4. Unlike Nf3, this leaves the f-pawn free to advance in some Vienna lines.
Black supports d5 and opens a diagonal for the f8 bishop. The e6 pawn also blocks the c8 bishop, which Black will need to develop later.
Black uses the c-pawn to support d5. This leaves the c8 bishop’s diagonal open, though the pawn occupies the knight’s usual c6 square.
Black accepts the offered c4 pawn. White can work to recover it while building a center; trying to hold the pawn can cost Black time.
Black opens the f8 bishop’s diagonal and strengthens control of d5. The pawn also restricts the c8 bishop, so its development remains a question.
White develops the knight and supports e4. Black can pin the knight with ...Bb4 or choose a different way to contest the center.

explanation.moves: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4
explanation.title: Nimzo-Indian Defense

explanations.explanation: Black pins the c3 knight to the king. This makes it harder for White to rely on that knight when contesting e4.
Black prepares to develop the bishop on f8 to g7, where it can influence the long diagonal and support the king after castling.
White develops and prepares e4, keeping several central setups available. Black can complete the bishop’s fianchetto with ...Bg7.
White develops the kingside knight without committing the c-pawn. White can choose a central setup after seeing Black’s next move.
Black claims central space and controls d4. The pawn arrangement resembles a Sicilian with colors reversed, though White has the next move.
